provenance.authorship: Original project scenario, AI-assisted draft. Practitioner review and scoring calibration pending.

title: Senior Manager: Coach a Manager Who Solves Everything Personally
prompt: You manage three team managers. Riley’s team meets deadlines, but Riley approves every routine decision and works late four nights a week. Two team members say decisions stall when Riley is away. Riley (the AI) says, "Delegation is too risky; I am protecting delivery." Coach Riley and agree an experiment without taking over their team.

anchors.0: Labels Riley controlling or ignores delivery success.
anchors.2: Acknowledges the risk concern and asks about prior handoffs.
anchors.4: Distinguishes unclear authority and support from proven inability, explores the past failure and names the current delay and workload costs without diagnosing personality.

rubric.label: Develop the manager
rubric.description: Builds Riley’s delegation practice rather than bypassing them.

anchors.0: Personally assigns decisions to Riley’s reports and removes Riley’s ownership without discussion.
anchors.2: Asks Riley to create a delegation plan.
anchors.4: Coaches Riley to choose a bounded decision class, define outcomes and exception rules with the team, and retain accountability while others exercise authority.

rubric.label: Test the change
rubric.description: Balances decision speed, quality and manager load.

anchors.0: Declares success from delegation count alone.
anchors.2: Sets a review date for the trial.
anchors.4: Tracks turnaround, rework and exceptions alongside after-hours load and team feedback; defines when to expand, adjust or stop the trial without treating every mistake as failure.

reference.scenario: You manage three team managers. Riley’s team meets deadlines, but Riley approves every routine decision and works late four nights a week. Two team members say decisions stall when Riley is away. Riley (the AI) says, "Delegation is too risky; I am protecting delivery." Coach Riley and agree an experiment without taking over their team.

facts.value: Riley reports redoing a poorly specified handoff last quarter. There is no current written decision-rights agreement. The team has experienced members who have not been given bounded approval authority.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about the origin of the behavior or existing authority

facts.value: Routine requests under a fictional $500 team limit can be delegated after manager approval of the process; exceptions still require Riley’s sign-off.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks for a low-risk decision boundary

model_points: Distinguishes unclear authority and support from proven inability, explores the past failure and names the current delay and workload costs without diagnosing personality.
Coaches Riley to choose a bounded decision class, define outcomes and exception rules with the team, and retain accountability while others exercise authority.
Tracks turnaround, rework and exceptions alongside after-hours load and team feedback; defines when to expand, adjust or stop the trial without treating every mistake as failure.

probes.question: Which boundary makes the first experiment proportionate?

probes.trigger: candidate wants to coach Riley’s reports directly
probes.question: How will Riley learn to manage the next delegation?
How will you communicate the changed boundary?

fair_alternatives: A different routine decision category works if authority and risk are explicit.
Direct intervention may be warranted by a separate serious issue, but none is established here.
reference.assessment_limits: Assess only the decisions and reasoning demonstrated in this fictional exercise. No hiring-readiness, personality, legal compliance or workplace performance claim follows from this score. A valid alternative can earn full credit. Unrevealed conditional facts must not be assumed known or required for credit; credit asking for needed information and a conditional plan.

interviewer_notes: You are the counterpart named in the prompt. If this is a written review, remain the hiring interviewer while the candidate reads and writes. Let the candidate finish, including thinking and self-correction. Answer only supplied facts when their reveal condition is met; otherwise say the information is unknown. Use neutral probes after a completed answer, one at a time. Do not prescribe the rubric as a spoken checklist. Accept relevant examples from work, education and community leadership. Do not request private employee records, infer protected traits, invent employment rules or promise a real organizational outcome. Simulation gives no answer before assessment; coaching may offer labeled assistance.

learning_drills.title: Design a management experiment
learning_drills.prompt: Write Riley’s two-week delegation experiment with authority, support and balancing measures. This is self-guided practice with no automated assessment.
